title: Warranty deductible temporary difference • case 10
prompt: A recognised warranty provision carries at LKR 450,000. The entire amount will be deductible only when paid, so its tax base is zero. Sufficient future taxable profit is probable and no recognition exception applies. The enacted rate on reversal is 30%. Find the deferred tax asset.
explanation: Liability tax base = carrying amount − future deduction = zero. Deductible temporary difference = 450,000; DTA = 450,000 × 30% = 135,000.00. Tax expense recognition and cash deduction occur in different periods.

title: Deferred tax expense bridge • case 10
prompt: Opening DTL is LKR 100,000 and closing DTL is 170,000. Opening DTA is 80,000 and closing DTA is 70,000. All changes belong in profit or loss, with no acquisitions, OCI, equity or foreign-exchange effects. Find deferred tax EXPENSE for the year.
explanation: Expense = increase in DTL + decrease in DTA = (170,000 − 100,000) + (80,000 − 70,000) = 80,000.00. Do not confuse the closing net balance with the period expense.

title: Tax loss recognition ceiling • case 10
prompt: Unused tax losses are LKR 1,000,000. Convincing evidence supports probable FUTURE taxable profit of only 600,000 before those losses expire. There are no other recovery sources or taxable temporary differences. Tax rate is 30%. Find the DTA that can be recognised on the losses.
explanation: Recognise only the losses supported by probable taxable profit: min(1,000,000, 600,000) × 30% = 180,000.00. The legal loss balance alone does not justify a larger asset.

title: Discounted VIU versus disposal value • case 10
prompt: An asset carries at LKR 1,400,000. Its appropriate value-in-use forecast is 400,000 received at each of the next three year ends, plus net disposal proceeds of 200,000 at year three. Appropriate discount rate is 10%. Fair value less costs of disposal is 850,000. No other cash flows or valuation adjustments apply. Find the impairment loss.
explanation: VIU = PV of three operating receipts plus PV of terminal disposal = 1,145,003.76. Recoverable amount is the HIGHER of VIU and 850,000: 1,145,003.76. Impairment = 1,400,000 − 1,145,003.76 = 254,996.24.

title: CGU residual pro-rata allocation • case 10
prompt: A CGU contains goodwill of LKR 150,000, asset A of 700,000, and asset B of 450,000. Recoverable amount is 850,000. No individual-asset floor restricts allocation and there are no other assets. Find asset B’s carrying amount AFTER allocating the CGU impairment.
explanation: Total impairment = 1,300,000 − 850,000 = 450,000. First eliminate goodwill of 150,000. Allocate remaining 300,000 pro rata to A and B. B loss = 117,391.30; closing B = 332,608.70.

title: CGU reversal without restoring goodwill • case 10
prompt: After past impairment, a CGU has assets A at LKR 600,000 and B at 400,000. All previously impaired goodwill is zero. Recoverable amount now rises to 1,250,000. A’s maximum permitted amount under its no-impairment ceiling is 660,000, and B’s is 520,000; no lower individual recoverable-amount limit applies. What is the maximum total CGU carrying amount after reversal?
explanation: Goodwill impairment is never reversed. The other assets cannot exceed their permitted ceilings: 660,000 + 520,000 = 1,180,000.00, below CGU recoverable amount 1,250,000. Allocate reversals subject to those ceilings.

title: Onerous contract least net exit cost • case 10

The alternative is to terminate now for a penalty of 400,000. No dedicated asset impairment is required and discounting is immaterial. Find the provision for the least net unavoidable cost.
explanation: Net cost of fulfilling = 1,700,000 − 1,050,000 = 650,000. Compare with termination penalty 400,000; the least net cost of exit is 400,000.00. Do not provide for gross fulfilment costs without expected benefits.
family: Onerous contract least net exit cost

title: Restructuring cost boundary • case 10
prompt: A qualifying restructuring has created the required present obligations. Direct supplier-contract cancellation penalties are LKR 250,000; legally required closure clean-up costs are 120,000. Planned staff retraining is 150,000, marketing is 80,000, and investment in new systems is 50,000 for continuing operations. No leases, employee termination benefits, other assets or discounting complications apply. What amount is included in the restructuring provision?
explanation: Include direct expenditures necessarily entailed by the restructuring and unrelated to ongoing activities: 250,000 + 120,000 = 370,000.00. Retraining, marketing and new-system investment for continuing business are excluded.

title: Inspection replacement and depreciation • case 10
prompt: On 1 January an asset’s carrying amount is LKR 1,100,000, including an old inspection component of 100,000. A new qualifying major inspection costs 240,000 that day and the old component is derecognised. The remaining main asset has four years’ life; the new inspection has three. Both use straight-line depreciation with zero residual value. Find total carrying amount at year end.

title: Commercial exchange gain • case 10

Fair value of the received equipment is not more clearly evident. No other costs or taxes apply. What GAIN is recognised on derecognising the equipment given?
explanation: Cost of received equipment = fair value given + cash = 1,400,000. The gain on the equipment surrendered is only its fair value minus carrying amount: 1,200,000 − 900,000 = 300,000.00. The cash paid is not a gain.

title: Periodic weighted average with discount • case 10
prompt: Opening inventory is 1,000 units at LKR 100 each. A purchase of 700 units is invoiced at 120 each with a 10% trade discount; inward freight is 2,000. Closing quantity is 600 units. Use periodic weighted average. NRV exceeds cost; there are no other movements or costs. Find closing inventory carrying amount.
explanation: Net purchase price per unit = 120 × 90% = 108. Total available cost = 100,000 + 700 × 108 + 2,000 = 177,600. Average = cost / 1,700 units. Closing value = average × 600 = 62,682.35.

title: Research expense and midyear amortisation • case 10

Find TOTAL current-year expense from these items; no impairment applies.

prompt: Cash consideration of LKR 1,300,000 covers delivered goods and loyalty points that are a separate material right. Stand-alone selling price of the goods is 1,000,000; the points’ estimated stand-alone price is 160,000, ALREADY adjusted for redemption probability. No points are redeemed yet. What contract liability is allocated to the points?
explanation: Allocate by relative stand-alone prices: 1,300,000 × 160,000 / 1,160,000 = 179,310.34. Do not apply redemption probability again; it is already included in the points’ stand-alone price.

title: Contract-cost asset impairment • case 12
prompt: A qualifying sales commission asset initially cost LKR 252,000 and is amortised evenly over three years. After one year of amortisation, expected remaining consideration for the related services is 1,020,000; directly related future fulfilment costs not yet expensed are 978,000. Other assets have already been tested and no further adjustment is required. Find the impairment loss on this contract-cost asset.
explanation: Post-amortisation carrying amount = 168,000.00. Recoverable benchmark = remaining consideration − related future costs = 42,000. Impairment = 168,000.00 − 42,000 = 126,000.00.

title: Non-distinct contract modification • case 12
prompt: A single over-time construction obligation had original price LKR 11,200,000. Revenue of 4,480,000.00 was recognised before modification. Approved added work is NOT distinct and adds 2,600,000 to the price. Under the appropriate input method the modified combined obligation is now 50% complete. No variable-price constraint or other issue applies. Find the cumulative catch-up revenue adjustment at modification.
explanation: Because added work is not distinct, update the existing combined obligation. Revised cumulative revenue = (11,200,000 + 2,600,000) × 50% = 6,900,000.00. Less previously recognised 4,480,000.00 gives an adjustment of 2,420,000.00.

title: Advance financing and revenue • case 12
prompt: A customer prepays LKR 1,300,000 exactly two years before goods transfer. The arrangement contains a significant financing component benefiting the supplier; the appropriate annual rate is 8%. No exemption applies. No other consideration or obligations exist. What revenue is recognised when control of the goods transfers?
explanation: Accrete the contract liability for two years: 1,300,000 × 1.08² = 1,516,320.00. The financing cost is recognised separately over the two years; the increased liability is released as revenue on transfer.

title: Upfront fee over the service term • case 12
prompt: A two-year service contract has a non-refundable joining fee of LKR 192,000 plus fixed monthly fees of 10,000 for 24 months. The joining activity transfers no separate service, all consideration relates to one evenly provided service obligation, and no renewal material right exists. Find revenue for the first six months of service.
explanation: Total transaction price = 192,000 + 24 × 10,000 = 432,000. The upfront activity is not a separate obligation. Recognise 6/24 of the total = 108,000.00.
family: Upfront fee over the service term

title: Credit-impaired net interest basis • case 12
prompt: A loan originated unimpaired subsequently became credit-impaired in the prior reporting period and remains so throughout the current year. Opening gross amortised cost is LKR 2,100,000; loss allowance is 420,000. Original effective rate is 9%. No cash flows or other opening adjustments occur. Find current-year interest revenue.
explanation: For this subsequently credit-impaired asset, apply the original EIR to amortised cost NET of allowance: (2,100,000 − 420,000) × 9% = 151,200.00. This is not the purchased/originated credit-impaired model.

title: Loan modification without derecognition • case 12
prompt: A financial asset is modified WITHOUT derecognition. Immediately before modification its gross carrying amount is LKR 1,240,000. Revised contractual receipts are 510,000 in one year and 596,000 in two years. Original EIR is 10%. Ignore fees and ECL changes. Find the modification LOSS recognised now.
explanation: Recompute gross carrying amount using the ORIGINAL EIR: 510,000/1.10 + 596,000/1.10² = 956,198.35. Modification loss = old gross amount 1,240,000 − 956,198.35 = 283,801.65.

title: Debt FVOCI residual movement • case 12
prompt: A debt investment at FVOCI opens with equal fair value and gross amortised cost of LKR 1,300,000, and no accumulated OCI. Current EIR interest is 104,000.00, coupon received is 72,000, and closing fair value is 1,498,000. No impairment, foreign exchange, purchases or disposals apply. Find the fair-value gain recognised in OCI for this year.
explanation: Closing amortised-cost benchmark = 1,300,000 + 104,000.00 − 72,000 = 1,332,000.00. OCI is fair value minus that benchmark = 1,498,000 − 1,332,000.00 = 166,000.00. EIR interest is profit or loss.

title: Debt extinguishment after settlement fees • case 12
prompt: A financial liability with carrying amount LKR 1,560,000 is fully extinguished by a cash settlement of 1,290,000 plus a fee of 26,000 paid to the lender as part of the settlement consideration. No replacement debt, other costs or equity component exists. Find the extinguishment GAIN.
explanation: Total consideration paid = 1,290,000 + lender settlement fee 26,000.00 = 1,316,000.00. Gain = liability carrying amount − total settlement consideration = 244,000.00.

title: Own-credit split on an FVTPL liability • case 12
prompt: A liability is designated at FVTPL under the eligible fair-value option. Its fair value increases by LKR 160,000, producing a total loss. Of this, 32,000 is attributable to improved own credit and qualifies for OCI presentation. The split does not create or enlarge an accounting mismatch. Find the loss recognised in PROFIT OR LOSS.
explanation: The eligible own-credit component of 32,000 goes to OCI. The remaining fair-value loss goes to profit or loss: 160,000 − 32,000 = 128,000.00. This presentation is for designated liabilities under the stated conditions.
family: Own-credit split on an FVTPL liability

title: Midyear acquisition and parent earnings • case 12
prompt: P acquires 80% of S on 1 October and reports to 31 December. P’s own annual profit is LKR 2,600,000, excluding any S dividend. S’s annual profit of 1,920,000 accrues evenly. Additional depreciation on acquisition-date fair-value adjustments for the POST-acquisition quarter is 52,000. No tax, intragroup trading, goodwill impairment or other adjustment exists. Find consolidated profit attributable to P’s owners.
explanation: Only post-acquisition profit enters: S’s quarter = 480,000.00; less FV depreciation 52,000 gives 428,000.00. Owners’ profit = 2,600,000 + 80% of adjusted quarter profit = 2,942,400.00.

title: Intragroup PPE transfer at year end • case 12
prompt: On 1 January P sells equipment to S for LKR 1,116,000; carrying amount in P was 744,000. Remaining useful life is three years with no residual value. S depreciates the transfer price straight-line for the full year. No tax or impairment applies. By how much must S’s closing PPE amount be REDUCED on consolidation to restore the group basis?
explanation: Eliminate transfer gain of 372,000, but reverse excess depreciation of 372,000/3 = 124,000.00. Net reduction in closing group PPE = 248,000.00. The intragroup sale does not create a group gain.
family: Intragroup PPE transfer at year end

title: Loss of control and retained interest • case 12
prompt: P loses control of S. Sale proceeds are LKR 2,600,000; fair value of the retained interest is 720,000; carrying NCI derecognised is 460,000. S’s consolidated net assets INCLUDING goodwill carry at 2,860,000. No accumulated OCI, transaction costs or other adjustment exists. Calculate the gain on loss of control.
explanation: Gain = proceeds + fair value retained + carrying NCI − subsidiary net assets including goodwill = 2,600,000 + 720,000 + 460,000 − 2,860,000 = 920,000.00.
family: Loss of control and retained interest

title: Buy more without losing control • case 12
prompt: P increases ownership of S from 80% to 90% and retains control. Carrying amount of the entire 20% NCI before purchase is LKR 520,000. P pays 420,000 for the additional 10% interest. No OCI or other changes exist. What amount is DEBITED to parent owners’ equity for the difference between consideration and NCI carrying amount acquired?
explanation: The purchased 10 percentage points are half of the previous 20% NCI. Derecognise NCI of 260,000.00. Debit parent equity for excess consideration: 420,000 − 260,000.00 = 160,000.00. There is no new goodwill or profit-or-loss charge.

title: Acquisition consideration at present value • case 12
prompt: An acquirer pays cash LKR 2,600,000 now, owes fixed consideration of 1,232,000 in one year, and has acquisition-date fair value of contingent consideration of 260,000. Discount fixed deferred consideration at 10%. NCI fair value is 500,000; identifiable net assets are 3,240,000. No previous holding or other adjustment applies. Find goodwill.
explanation: Deferred consideration PV = 1,232,000/1.10 = 1,120,000.00. Goodwill = upfront + discounted fixed consideration + contingent FV + NCI − identifiable net assets = 1,240,000.00. Later financing unwinding is separate.

title: Acquisition uplift and deferred tax • case 12
prompt: Consideration is LKR 3,600,000; NCI is measured at fair value of 600,000. Identifiable net assets before an equipment uplift are 3,040,000. Acquisition-date equipment uplift is 520,000, with no tax-base uplift. Tax rate on reversal is 30%; no DTL exception applies. No other adjustment exists. Find goodwill after recognising the uplift and related DTL.
explanation: DTL on uplift = 520,000 × 30% = 156,000.00. Net identifiable assets = 3,040,000 + 520,000 − DTL = 3,404,000.00. Goodwill = consideration + NCI − net identifiable assets = 796,000.00.

title: Measurement-period goodwill adjustment • case 12
prompt: Provisional goodwill was LKR 1,240,000. During the measurement period, new information about acquisition-date facts establishes an additional identifiable equipment fair-value uplift of 260,000. The tax base is unchanged and a 30% DTL must be recognised. NCI was measured at fair value and that value is unchanged. All other acquisition amounts are final. Find revised acquisition-date goodwill.
explanation: Additional net identifiable assets = uplift − 30% DTL = 182,000.00. Retrospectively reduce goodwill by that net amount: 1,240,000 − 182,000.00 = 1,058,000.00. Subsequent equipment depreciation is considered separately.

title: Advance rent and initial ROU cost • case 12
prompt: A three-year lease has three equal annual payments of LKR 210,000 each: one at commencement, one in a year and one in two years. Discount rate is 10%. Initial direct costs are 20,000 and incentives received at commencement are 5,000. No restoration obligation exists. Find initial ROU asset cost.
explanation: Initial liability excludes the payment already made: 210,000/1.10 + 210,000/1.10² = 364,462.81. ROU = liability + commencement payment + direct costs − incentive = 589,462.81.
family: Advance rent and initial ROU cost

title: Index-linked payment remeasurement • case 12
prompt: A CPI change triggers a lessee remeasurement. Immediately before it, lease liability is LKR 212,000. The revised remaining payments are 135,520 in one year and the same amount in two years. The original 10% discount rate remains appropriate; no floating-interest-rate change or modification applies. Find the INCREASE in liability, normally adjusting the ROU asset.
explanation: Revised liability = 135,520/1.10 + 135,520/1.10² = 235,200.00. For this index change retain the original discount rate. Increase = revised liability − 212,000 = 23,200.00.

title: Partial termination and remaining ROU • case 12
prompt: A lease modification reduces scope by 40%, with a proportionate reduction in the ROU asset and liability. Immediately before modification, ROU carrying amount is LKR 1,140,000 and liability 1,240,000. After accounting for termination, remeasuring the remaining payments at the revised appropriate rate gives a liability of 800,000. No impairment applies. Find the FINAL ROU carrying amount after both steps.
explanation: First retain 60% of the ROU (684,000.00) and liability (744,000.00), recognising the termination difference in profit or loss. Then adjust ROU by revised liability minus remaining liability: 56,000.00. Final ROU = 740,000.00.

title: Finance lessor effective interest • case 12
prompt: A finance lessor’s net investment comprises four year-end rentals of LKR 420,000 and an unguaranteed residual of 160,000 recovered at the end of year four. The interest rate implicit in the lease is 8%. No initial direct costs outside those reflected in this rate, credit losses or other adjustments exist. Find finance income for the first year, BEFORE the first rental is received.
explanation: Initial net investment = PV of the four rentals plus PV of residual = 1,508,698.05. First-year finance income = opening net investment × 8% = 120,695.84, giving a constant periodic return.

title: Warranty deductible temporary difference • case 12
prompt: A recognised warranty provision carries at LKR 480,000. The entire amount will be deductible only when paid, so its tax base is zero. Sufficient future taxable profit is probable and no recognition exception applies. The enacted rate on reversal is 30%. Find the deferred tax asset.
explanation: Liability tax base = carrying amount − future deduction = zero. Deductible temporary difference = 480,000; DTA = 480,000 × 30% = 144,000.00. Tax expense recognition and cash deduction occur in different periods.

title: Deferred tax expense bridge • case 12
prompt: Opening DTL is LKR 100,000 and closing DTL is 174,000. Opening DTA is 80,000 and closing DTA is 72,000. All changes belong in profit or loss, with no acquisitions, OCI, equity or foreign-exchange effects. Find deferred tax EXPENSE for the year.
explanation: Expense = increase in DTL + decrease in DTA = (174,000 − 100,000) + (80,000 − 72,000) = 82,000.00. Do not confuse the closing net balance with the period expense.

title: Tax loss recognition ceiling • case 12
prompt: Unused tax losses are LKR 1,040,000. Convincing evidence supports probable FUTURE taxable profit of only 620,000 before those losses expire. There are no other recovery sources or taxable temporary differences. Tax rate is 30%. Find the DTA that can be recognised on the losses.
explanation: Recognise only the losses supported by probable taxable profit: min(1,040,000, 620,000) × 30% = 186,000.00. The legal loss balance alone does not justify a larger asset.

title: Discounted VIU versus disposal value • case 12
prompt: An asset carries at LKR 1,440,000. Its appropriate value-in-use forecast is 420,000 received at each of the next three year ends, plus net disposal proceeds of 200,000 at year three. Appropriate discount rate is 10%. Fair value less costs of disposal is 850,000. No other cash flows or valuation adjustments apply. Find the impairment loss.
explanation: VIU = PV of three operating receipts plus PV of terminal disposal = 1,194,740.80. Recoverable amount is the HIGHER of VIU and 850,000: 1,194,740.80. Impairment = 1,440,000 − 1,194,740.80 = 245,259.20.

title: CGU residual pro-rata allocation • case 12
prompt: A CGU contains goodwill of LKR 150,000, asset A of 720,000, and asset B of 460,000. Recoverable amount is 860,000. No individual-asset floor restricts allocation and there are no other assets. Find asset B’s carrying amount AFTER allocating the CGU impairment.
explanation: Total impairment = 1,330,000 − 860,000 = 470,000. First eliminate goodwill of 150,000. Allocate remaining 320,000 pro rata to A and B. B loss = 124,745.76; closing B = 335,254.24.

title: CGU reversal without restoring goodwill • case 12
prompt: After past impairment, a CGU has assets A at LKR 600,000 and B at 400,000. All previously impaired goodwill is zero. Recoverable amount now rises to 1,260,000. A’s maximum permitted amount under its no-impairment ceiling is 662,000, and B’s is 524,000; no lower individual recoverable-amount limit applies. What is the maximum total CGU carrying amount after reversal?
explanation: Goodwill impairment is never reversed. The other assets cannot exceed their permitted ceilings: 662,000 + 524,000 = 1,186,000.00, below CGU recoverable amount 1,260,000. Allocate reversals subject to those ceilings.

title: Onerous contract least net exit cost • case 12
prompt: A contract has a present onerous obligation. Directly related costs to fulfil are LKR 1,740,000, while expected contract benefits are 1,060,000. The alternative is to terminate now for a penalty of 420,000. No dedicated asset impairment is required and discounting is immaterial. Find the provision for the least net unavoidable cost.
explanation: Net cost of fulfilling = 1,740,000 − 1,060,000 = 680,000. Compare with termination penalty 420,000; the least net cost of exit is 420,000.00. Do not provide for gross fulfilment costs without expected benefits.
family: Onerous contract least net exit cost

title: Restructuring cost boundary • case 12
prompt: A qualifying restructuring has created the required present obligations. Direct supplier-contract cancellation penalties are LKR 260,000; legally required closure clean-up costs are 124,000. Planned staff retraining is 150,000, marketing is 80,000, and investment in new systems is 50,000 for continuing operations. No leases, employee termination benefits, other assets or discounting complications apply. What amount is included in the restructuring provision?
explanation: Include direct expenditures necessarily entailed by the restructuring and unrelated to ongoing activities: 260,000 + 124,000 = 384,000.00. Retraining, marketing and new-system investment for continuing business are excluded.

title: Inspection replacement and depreciation • case 12
prompt: On 1 January an asset’s carrying amount is LKR 1,140,000, including an old inspection component of 100,000. A new qualifying major inspection costs 252,000 that day and the old component is derecognised. The remaining main asset has four years’ life; the new inspection has three. Both use straight-line depreciation with zero residual value. Find total carrying amount at year end.
explanation: Derecognise old inspection: main asset = 1,040,000. Depreciate main asset by 260,000.00 and new inspection by 84,000.00. Closing = 780,000.00 + 168,000.00 = 948,000.00.

title: Commercial exchange gain • case 12
prompt: An equipment exchange has commercial substance. The entity gives equipment with carrying amount LKR 920,000 and reliably measurable fair value 1,240,000, plus 200,000 cash. Fair value of the received equipment is not more clearly evident. No other costs or taxes apply. What GAIN is recognised on derecognising the equipment given?
explanation: Cost of received equipment = fair value given + cash = 1,440,000. The gain on the equipment surrendered is only its fair value minus carrying amount: 1,240,000 − 920,000 = 320,000.00. The cash paid is not a gain.

title: Periodic weighted average with discount • case 12
prompt: Opening inventory is 1,000 units at LKR 100 each. A purchase of 740 units is invoiced at 120 each with a 10% trade discount; inward freight is 2,000. Closing quantity is 620 units. Use periodic weighted average. NRV exceeds cost; there are no other movements or costs. Find closing inventory carrying amount.
explanation: Net purchase price per unit = 120 × 90% = 108. Total available cost = 100,000 + 740 × 108 + 2,000 = 181,920. Average = cost / 1,740 units. Closing value = average × 620 = 64,822.07.

title: Net acquisition cash flow • case 12
prompt: A subsidiary acquisition involves cash consideration PAID this year of LKR 1,600,000, plus deferred consideration of 200,000 not yet paid. Cash and cash equivalents acquired with the subsidiary are 160,000; acquired borrowings are 300,000. No fees or other cash payments occur. Find the net INVESTING cash outflow from obtaining control.
explanation: Cash flow from obtaining control is investing, reported net of cash and cash equivalents acquired: 1,600,000 − 160,000 = 1,440,000.00 outflow. Unpaid deferred consideration and assumed debt are not cash payments in this case.

title: Research expense and midyear amortisation • case 12
prompt: In the current year a project incurs research costs LKR 92,000, development spending of 50,000 before recognition criteria are met, then qualifying development cost of 840,000. The completed asset becomes available for use on 1 July, has a five-year finite life and zero residual value. Use six months of straight-line amortisation. Find TOTAL current-year expense from these items; no impairment applies.
explanation: Expense research and pre-recognition development: 92,000 + 50,000. Capitalise 840,000, then amortise for six months: 840,000/5 × 6/12 = 84,000.00. Total expense = 226,000.00.

title: Associate upstream adjusted earnings • case 12
prompt: An investor owns 30% of an associate. Associate profit is LKR 740,000. The investor’s equity-method adjustments include extra depreciation of 124,000 on acquisition-date fair values, and an upstream inventory sale leaves unrealised profit of 72,000 in the investor’s inventory. No tax, basis differences beyond those stated, impairment or other adjustments apply. Find the equity-accounted share of profit after both adjustments.
explanation: Adjust associate result before taking the share: 740,000 − 124,000 − 72,000 = 544,000. Investor’s share = 30% × adjusted result = 163,200.00. The investor’s share of upstream unrealised profit is eliminated.

title: Substantive customer acceptance
prompt: A bespoke machine cannot be shown to meet the customer’s objectively specified criteria before testing. Acceptance is substantive and remains outstanding. What is the key revenue implication?
options: Control may not have transferred until substantive acceptance is obtained
A sales target overrides acceptance terms
Cash receipt always makes acceptance irrelevant
explanation: Assess whether acceptance is substantive. If compliance cannot be objectively established before acceptance, the seller may be unable to conclude that control has transferred.

title: Assurance-only warranty
prompt: A product warranty cannot be purchased separately and only assures the product complies with agreed specifications. No extra service is provided. Which framework generally addresses the warranty obligation?
options: LKAS 37 rather than a separate SLFRS 15 performance obligation
SLFRS 16 because the customer uses the product
explanation: An assurance-type warranty is accounted for under LKAS 37 unless it provides a service in addition to assurance.

title: Separately sold extended warranty
prompt: A customer can purchase an extended warranty separately, providing an additional maintenance service. How should its consideration generally be treated?
options: Allocate consideration to a separate service performance obligation
Recognise the entire warranty price as product revenue immediately
Deduct the price from share capital
Ignore the warranty because no fault has occurred yet
explanation: A separately purchasable warranty is a distinct service. Its allocated consideration is recognised as that service is provided.

title: Paying the customer for nothing distinct
prompt: A supplier pays a customer a listing allowance but receives no distinct good or service in return. What is the general treatment?
options: Reduce transaction price and revenue under the relevant timing requirements
Always recognise a separate intangible asset
Recognise extra revenue for the payment
explanation: Consideration payable to a customer generally reduces transaction price and revenue unless it pays for a distinct good or service received.

title: Non-cash consideration
prompt: A customer promises a reliably measurable asset in exchange for a service. Which general transaction-price basis applies to that non-cash consideration?
options: Fair value of the non-cash consideration, subject to the standard’s requirements
Always the customer’s original asset cost
Always zero until it is sold for cash
The service provider’s desired margin alone
explanation: Non-cash consideration is measured at fair value. If fair value cannot be reasonably estimated, the indirect stand-alone selling-price approach applies.

title: Collectability at contract inception
prompt: Enforceable promises and payment terms exist, but collecting the consideration to which the entity expects to be entitled is not probable. Do the ordinary contract-accounting criteria automatically apply?
options: No; the collectability criterion and other contract requirements must be met
Yes; enforceable signatures are the only criterion
Yes; every quotation is a revenue contract
No; credit sales are never revenue contracts
explanation: The contract criteria include probable collection, considering the customer’s ability and intention to pay the consideration expected in exchange for transfer.

title: A deposit after contract criteria fail
prompt: Cash is received for an arrangement that does not yet meet the contract criteria. Promised goods remain untransferred and the relevant conditions for revenue on termination or completed obligations are not met. What follows?
options: Continue recognising the receipt as a liability
Recognise revenue because the receipt is labelled non-refundable
Recognise goodwill equal to the deposit
Credit the deposit directly to retained earnings
explanation: When the contract criteria are not met, consideration received remains a liability until the specified conditions for revenue recognition are satisfied or the contract criteria are later met.

title: Licence giving a right to access
prompt: A licence meets the criteria for a right to access the entity’s intellectual property as it exists throughout the licence period. What revenue pattern generally follows?
options: Recognise revenue over time using an appropriate progress measure
Recognise all revenue as soon as the agreement is signed
Recognise revenue only on the last day regardless of performance
Treat every licence as a lease of PPE
explanation: A qualifying right-to-access licence is a performance obligation satisfied over time; a right-to-use licence is assessed differently.

title: Recourse can retain exposure
prompt: An entity transfers receivables but retains substantially all credit risk through a comprehensive recourse guarantee. What is the general derecognition implication?
options: Continue recognising the receivables and account for the proceeds as a liability as appropriate
Always derecognise because legal title moved
Recognise only the guarantee and erase every receivable
Recognise the proceeds as ordinary revenue
explanation: When substantially all risks and rewards are retained, the transferred asset continues to be recognised; the transfer proceeds do not by themselves establish derecognition.

title: Regular-way purchase policy
prompt: A regular-way financial-asset purchase is within the relevant requirements. Which recognition timing approach is permitted?
options: Trade-date or settlement-date accounting, applied consistently for the relevant category
Any date selected to maximise quarterly profit
Only the date the investment is eventually sold
Only year end regardless of purchase timing
explanation: Regular-way purchases and sales use trade-date or settlement-date accounting, applied consistently within the required measurement category.

title: The fair-value option is deliberate
prompt: A qualifying financial asset would otherwise be amortised cost, but designation at FVTPL at initial recognition eliminates or significantly reduces an accounting mismatch. What characteristic does the election have?
options: It is an eligible irrevocable initial-recognition designation
It can be changed every month for profit smoothing
It replaces the need to assess contractual cash flows in every case
It automatically changes every group investment to FVTPL
explanation: The specified fair-value option is an irrevocable designation at initial recognition when the accounting-mismatch condition is met.

title: Reasonable prepayment compensation
prompt: A basic lending instrument permits early repayment of principal, accrued interest and reasonable compensation for early termination. Is that clause alone necessarily fatal to SPPI?
options: No; the relevant prepayment requirements allow qualifying compensation
Yes; every prepayment clause fails SPPI
Yes; only perpetual debt can pass SPPI
No; all equity-index-linked prepayments always pass
explanation: Certain prepayment terms can be consistent with principal and interest, including reasonable compensation for early termination, subject to the detailed requirements.

title: What twelve-month ECL means
prompt: An analyst measures twelve-month ECL as only cash shortfalls expected to be collected during the next twelve months. What correction is needed?
options: Use lifetime cash shortfalls arising from defaults possible within the next twelve months, probability weighted
Ignore defaults until twelve months have passed
Use only next month’s unpaid interest
Recognise exactly one year of contractual coupons as the allowance
explanation: Twelve-month ECL is the portion of lifetime ECL resulting from default events possible within twelve months after reporting date, not merely shortfalls during that twelve-month cash window.

title: Forward-looking evidence in ECL
prompt: A lender has reliable forecasts of worsening economic conditions but uses only historic default percentages without adjustment. What must its ECL assessment consider?
options: Reasonable and supportable past, current and forecast information available without undue cost or effort
Only the oldest available loss history
explanation: ECL is forward looking and uses reasonable supportable information, including forecasts, alongside past events and current conditions.

title: Writing off an exhausted recovery
prompt: An entity has no reasonable expectation of recovering all or part of a financial asset. What does the standard require for that exhausted portion?
options: Directly reduce its gross carrying amount by a write-off
Keep the gross asset forever as long as a legal claim exists
Reclassify the amount as an equity investment
Recognise the loss only when all court proceedings end
explanation: A write-off occurs when there is no reasonable expectation of recovery; it is a derecognition event and can apply to all or part of the asset.

title: Transaction costs follow classification
prompt: A dealer acquires an asset measured at FVTPL and incurs directly attributable transaction costs. How are those costs generally treated?
options: Expense them rather than add them to initial FVTPL carrying amount
Capitalise them in every FVTPL asset
Deduct them from the issuer’s share capital
explanation: Initial measurement adds or subtracts directly attributable transaction costs only for instruments not at FVTPL. FVTPL transaction costs are expensed.

title: Different subsidiary reporting date
prompt: It is impracticable for a subsidiary to prepare statements at the parent’s reporting date. The difference is no more than three months. What additional condition is relevant?
options: Adjust for significant transactions or events between dates and maintain the permitted consistent date difference
Use any reporting date difference without limit
explanation: The standard permits the specified limited reporting-date difference when necessary, with adjustments for significant intervening transactions and events and consistency requirements.

title: Temporary control remains control
prompt: A parent controls a subsidiary and plans to sell it soon. No consolidation exception applies. Does the planned short holding period alone remove the consolidation requirement?
options: No; consolidate while control exists and apply held-for-sale rules when appropriate
Yes; every investment held less than a year is exempt
Yes; intent to sell creates an associate automatically
No; it must remain consolidated after control is lost too
explanation: Control determines consolidation. A planned sale does not itself create an exemption; relevant SLFRS 5 requirements may also apply.

title: Intragroup dividend elimination
prompt: A subsidiary pays a dividend to its parent, which recognised dividend income in separate accounts. What is required in consolidated profit or loss?
options: Retain it as new group revenue
Recognise the same dividend twice as investment income
Treat it as a gain on disposal of goodwill
explanation: Intragroup income, expenses and related transactions are eliminated in full. A subsidiary-to-parent dividend does not create income from outside the group.

title: NCI may become negative
prompt: A subsidiary’s losses allocated to NCI exceed the NCI’s opening equity. What general allocation principle applies?
options: Attribute the losses to NCI even if this creates a deficit balance
Stop allocating all losses to NCI at zero in every case
Charge all further losses only to goodwill
explanation: Profit or loss and each component of OCI are attributed to owners and NCI even if attribution results in an NCI deficit balance.

title: Control is reassessed
prompt: A shareholder agreement changes substantive decision rights during the year. What should an investor do?
options: Reassess control when facts and circumstances indicate changes to its elements
Wait for the next purchase of shares in every case
Assess only whether dividends were received
explanation: An investor reassesses control if facts and circumstances indicate changes to one or more of its elements.

title: Low value is assessed on a new basis
prompt: A lessee considers the low-value-asset exemption for an old asset that originally had a high value when new. Does its low second-hand price alone establish eligibility?
options: No; assess the value of the underlying asset when new under the exemption’s requirements
Yes; any low used price establishes eligibility
Yes; every asset used by an SME qualifies
No; the exemption depends only on the lessee’s annual revenue
explanation: The low-value assessment is based on the asset’s value when new and the other specified conditions, not merely a low current resale price.

title: An extension that matters
prompt: A lessee has an extension option and strong economic incentives make exercise reasonably certain. How is the extension period generally treated?
options: Include it in the lease term
Include only if the option has already been formally exercised
Treat it as a separate intangible asset
explanation: The lease term includes extension periods when the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise the option, considering relevant facts and economic incentives.

title: An identifiable portion
prompt: A contract gives use of a physically distinct floor in a building, with the other lease criteria met. Can that portion be an identified asset?
options: Yes; a physically distinct portion can be an identified asset
No; only whole buildings can be leased
Only if the customer buys the land
No; every portion is automatically a service
explanation: A capacity portion can be an identified asset when physically distinct. A non-distinct portion is generally not identified unless it represents substantially all capacity.

title: Sublease classification basis
prompt: An intermediate lessor classifies a sublease and the head lease is not accounted for under the short-term exemption. What asset generally anchors classification?
options: The ROU asset arising from the head lease
Always the underlying asset’s original full economic life alone
explanation: An intermediate lessor classifies a sublease with reference to the head-lease ROU asset, with the specified exception for exempt short-term head leases.

title: Commencement differs from signing
prompt: A lease is signed in November, but the lessor makes the asset available for use only in January. When does the lessee generally recognise its ROU asset and lease liability?
options: Automatically at the November signature date
Only when the first sale is made using the asset
Only at the end of the first financial year
explanation: Commencement is the date the lessor makes the underlying asset available for use; lessee recognition occurs at commencement.

title: Common control scope
prompt: A business combination is between entities under common control before and after the transaction, and that control is not transitory. What scope issue arises?
options: It is outside SLFRS 3’s business-combination requirements
SLFRS 3 mandates a new goodwill asset in every case
It is automatically an asset disposal to an outsider
Common control removes every accounting policy requirement
explanation: Business combinations of entities or businesses under common control are excluded from SLFRS 3’s scope; an appropriate policy must be determined under the applicable framework.

title: Acquired contingent liability recognition
prompt: An acquired item is a present obligation from past events with reliably measurable fair value, but an outflow is not probable. Which acquisition exception is relevant?
options: A qualifying acquired contingent liability can be recognised even without probable outflow
It is always excluded because LKAS 37 probability must apply unchanged
It is recognised only when cash is paid
It is always classified as goodwill itself
explanation: For a qualifying present obligation acquired in a business combination, SLFRS 3 can require contingent-liability recognition despite the ordinary probability criterion not being met.

title: Indemnified acquired exposure
prompt: The seller contractually indemnifies the acquirer for a recognised acquired liability. What is the general basis for recognising the indemnification asset?
options: Use a basis consistent with the indemnified item, considering collectability and contractual limits
Always measure it at unlimited nominal exposure
Always net it against goodwill with no separate assessment
Recognise it only when the seller pays cash
explanation: An indemnification asset is recognised at the same time as the indemnified item using consistent assumptions, subject to collectability and contractual limitations.

title: Goodwill after acquisition
prompt: A group applies full SLFRSs to recognised goodwill. Which subsequent approach is appropriate?
options: Do not amortise goodwill; apply required impairment testing
Amortise it automatically over five years
Revalue goodwill upward each year to market value
Expense it only when the group chooses to sell
explanation: Goodwill recognised in a business combination is not amortised under full SLFRSs and is subject to LKAS 36 impairment requirements.

title: Tax follows the underlying item
prompt: A tax consequence relates to an item recognised directly in OCI. No exception changes the allocation. Where should that related tax effect be recognised?
options: In OCI, consistently with the underlying item
Always as an operating expense in profit or loss
Always in current tax payable only without an expense effect
explanation: Tax consequences of items recognised outside profit or loss are also recognised outside profit or loss, in OCI or directly in equity as appropriate.

title: Deferred tax is not discounted
prompt: A temporary difference reverses many years in the future. Does that timing by itself permit discounting the recognised deferred tax balance?
options: No; deferred tax assets and liabilities are not discounted
Yes; discounting is mandatory for every deferred tax balance
Only deferred tax liabilities may be discounted
Only deferred tax assets may be discounted
explanation: LKAS 12 expressly prohibits discounting deferred tax assets and liabilities.

title: Current tax offset is conditional
prompt: Two group entities have current tax balances but no legally enforceable right to set them off. Can consolidated ownership alone justify offsetting?
options: No; the current-tax offset requirements must be satisfied
Yes; consolidation always permits tax netting
Yes; matching tax rates are sufficient
Yes; any common accountant can authorise it
explanation: Current tax offset requires a legally enforceable set-off right and the relevant intention to settle net or realise and settle simultaneously.

title: Advance revenue already taxed
prompt: An entity has a contract liability because cash was received before service. That receipt has already been taxed, and the future accounting revenue will not be taxed again. Which tax-base principle is relevant?
options: The liability tax base excludes the amount of future revenue that will not be taxable
The tax base must always equal the cash received
Tax base always equals zero for every liability irrespective of tax law
Recognise the same receipt as taxable income again automatically
explanation: For revenue received in advance, liability tax base is its carrying amount less revenue that will not be taxable in future periods. This can create a deductible temporary difference.

title: Do not use the wrong impairment model
prompt: A trade receivable is within the SLFRS 9 expected-credit-loss requirements. Should its allowance be measured under LKAS 36’s ordinary recoverable-amount model instead?
options: No; apply the impairment requirements of SLFRS 9
Yes; LKAS 36 overrides every other impairment standard
Only if the receivable is denominated in LKR
Yes; all asset losses use value in use
explanation: LKAS 36 excludes assets whose impairment is addressed by specified other standards, including financial assets under SLFRS 9.

title: The smallest independent cash inflows
prompt: An asset cannot be tested individually because its recoverable amount cannot be determined. How is the relevant CGU identified?
options: Use the smallest identifiable group generating largely independent cash inflows
Use the entire legal group in every case
Use the highest-profit business to absorb every loss
Use only the asset’s department name
explanation: A CGU is the smallest identifiable group with cash inflows largely independent of other assets or groups, subject to the standard’s requirements.

title: Impairment of a revalued asset
prompt: A revalued PPE item is impaired and has an available revaluation surplus for that same asset. How is the impairment generally recognised?
options: As a revaluation decrease under the applicable standard to the extent relevant, with any excess in profit or loss
Always entirely as a new goodwill balance
Never recognise an impairment for a revalued asset
explanation: An impairment loss on a revalued asset is treated as a revaluation decrease in accordance with the relevant standard.

title: Annual goodwill test timing
prompt: A CGU with goodwill is tested annually at a date selected by the entity. What timing discipline applies?
options: Test at the same time each year, with additional testing when indicators arise
Change the date whenever a loss appears likely
Skip testing whenever the parent pays dividends
explanation: Annual impairment testing can be performed at any time during the annual period provided it is performed at the same time every year; indicator-triggered testing also applies.

title: Unwinding is not a new surprise loss
prompt: A discounted provision increases solely because one year passes. What is the general treatment of that increase?
options: Recognise it as a borrowing cost from unwinding the discount
Recognise it as a reduction of sales revenue
Recognise it only in a revaluation reserve
explanation: For discounted provisions, the carrying amount increases as settlement approaches; the passage-of-time increase is recognised as a borrowing cost.

title: Do not net a merely possible recovery
prompt: A provision meets recognition criteria. An unrelated claim against a third party may produce recovery but is not virtually certain. What is appropriate?
options: Keep the recognised provision and do not recognise or net an unsupported recovery asset
Reduce the provision by the full hoped-for claim
Recognise every possible recovery as cash
Remove the provision until the claim is resolved
explanation: A provision and potential reimbursement are assessed separately. A reimbursement asset requires virtual certainty on settlement; possible recovery cannot justify netting an unsupported amount.

title: Review every reporting date
prompt: Updated evidence shows that an outflow for a previously recognised provision is no longer probable. What must be considered?
options: Reverse the provision when an outflow is no longer probable
Keep the provision permanently as a hidden reserve
Transfer it automatically to share capital
Increase it because uncertainty has fallen
explanation: Provisions are reviewed each reporting date and adjusted to the current best estimate; when an outflow is no longer probable, the provision is reversed.

title: Revenue is not a depreciation driver
prompt: A manufacturer proposes depreciation solely as a fixed percentage of selling revenue. The method does not reflect consumption of the asset’s economic benefits. What is the standard’s conclusion?
options: A revenue-based depreciation method is not appropriate
Revenue must always be the only depreciation base
Depreciation stops whenever selling prices fall
explanation: Depreciation reflects the pattern of consumption of economic benefits; a method based on revenue generated by an activity is not appropriate.

title: Initial restoration estimate in cost
prompt: Acquiring equipment creates a recognised obligation to dismantle it and restore the site. The obligation is not related to producing inventory during a later period. What enters initial equipment cost?
options: The initial estimate of the qualifying dismantling and restoration obligation
Only future cash actually paid many years later
Nothing because the payment is not immediate
explanation: PPE cost includes the initial estimate of dismantling, removal and restoration obligations under the specified conditions; the related liability is measured under LKAS 37.

title: Idle does not mean non-depreciable
prompt: A depreciable machine becomes temporarily idle but is not derecognised or classified as held for sale, and depreciation is not zero under its applicable method. What is the general implication?
options: Do not stop depreciation merely because it is idle
Always stop depreciation until the first new order
Reclassify the machine as cash equivalent
explanation: Depreciation does not cease when an asset is idle or retired from active use unless fully depreciated, although a usage-based method may produce a zero charge when there is no production.

title: Three months from acquisition
prompt: A company buys a six-month investment that has only two months remaining at year end. Is the remaining year-end maturity alone sufficient to make it a cash equivalent?
options: No; short maturity is normally assessed from acquisition, together with the other cash-equivalent conditions
Yes; every investment maturing within three months after year end qualifies
Yes; every interest-bearing asset is a cash equivalent
No; cash equivalents can never earn interest
explanation: Cash equivalents are short-term highly liquid investments meeting the specified criteria; a short maturity is normally three months or less from acquisition, not from reporting date.

title: Financing liabilities reconciliation
prompt: A reconciliation of liabilities arising from financing activities includes both cash-flow movements and non-cash changes. Why?
options: It enables users to evaluate changes in financing liabilities, including cash and non-cash changes
Every change in a loan is necessarily a cash flow
It replaces all financing cash-flow disclosures
It permits non-cash movements to be counted as cash receipts
explanation: The financing-liabilities disclosure explains changes from cash flows and non-cash changes such as acquisitions, exchange differences and fair-value movements.

title: Specific identification for unique projects
prompt: An entity holds non-interchangeable units specifically segregated for individual projects. What cost assignment is appropriate?
options: A selling-price percentage regardless of actual cost
Automatic use of group-wide average prices for unlike units
explanation: Specific identification applies to non-interchangeable items and goods or services produced and segregated for specific projects.

title: Storage cost boundary
prompt: Storage is not necessary in the production process before a further production stage. What is the normal inventory-cost treatment?
options: Exclude the storage cost and expense it
explanation: Storage costs are generally excluded from inventory cost unless necessary in the production process before a further production stage.

title: Advertising does not create a brand asset
prompt: A company spends heavily on advertising for its internally generated brand. The spending does not create a separately recognisable purchased intangible. What is appropriate?
options: Expense advertising under the applicable recognition requirements rather than recognise the internally generated brand
Capitalise the whole campaign automatically as a brand
Recognise the brand at management’s desired valuation
Recognise an asset because all advertising promises future sales
explanation: Internally generated brands are not recognised as intangible assets; advertising and promotional expenditure is generally expensed when the relevant goods or services are received.

title: Significant influence ends
prompt: An investor loses significant influence and retains a financial asset within SLFRS 9. What is the general treatment of that retained interest at the date influence ceases?
options: Measure the retained interest at fair value and apply the specified discontinuation gain-or-loss calculation
Keep applying the equity method forever
Always keep the original acquisition cost without assessment
explanation: When equity-method accounting ceases and the retained interest is a financial asset, fair value is used at that date and the resulting difference is recognised under the specified requirements.

title: Operating is not just recurring core activity
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. A manufacturer incurs an unusual litigation expense that belongs to none of the other four profit-or-loss categories. Where does it go?
explanation: The operating category is residual: it includes income and expenses not classified in investing, financing, income taxes or discontinued operations. Unusual or non-recurring does not automatically mean non-operating.

title: Equity-method result stays investing
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. An entity invests in associates as a main business activity. The associate is accounted for using the equity method. Where is the share of its profit classified?
options: Operating merely because investing is a main activity
explanation: Even for the specified main-business-activity case, income and expenses from equity-method investments are classified in investing.

title: Rental property outside the main business
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. A manufacturer holds investment property generating returns largely independently of its other resources. Investing in such property is not a main business activity. Where is related rental income generally classified?
options: Discontinued operations regardless of sale plans
explanation: Returns from independently generating assets are generally investing unless the specified main-business-activity requirements change classification.

title: Customer financing is the bank’s business
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. A bank provides financing to customers as a main business activity. Where is interest income from those customer loans generally classified?
options: Investing solely because it is interest
Financing solely because it is interest
explanation: The specified main-business-activity rules move relevant returns from financing customers to operating rather than applying the ordinary independent-asset classification mechanically.

title: Funding the customer-finance business
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. A bank’s borrowing arises only from raising finance and relates to its main business of providing financing to customers. Where are the specified borrowing income and expenses classified?
options: Financing in every entity without exception
explanation: For an entity providing financing to customers as a main activity, the specified income and expenses from related pure-financing liabilities are operating.

title: Insurance finance is an explicit exception
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. Insurance finance expenses are included in profit or loss under SLFRS 17. Which SLFRS 18 category applies under the explicit exception?
options: Financing simply because the item is called finance
explanation: SLFRS 18 explicitly excludes the specified SLFRS 17 insurance finance income and expenses from financing and classifies them in operating.

title: Provision unwinding classification
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. A manufacturer separately identifies interest expense from unwinding a restoration provision when applying LKAS 37. No special exception applies. Where is that interest generally classified?
options: Operating solely because restoration relates to a factory
explanation: For liabilities not arising solely from raising finance, separately identified interest under other standards is classified in financing under the specified rules.

title: Borrowing exchange differences
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. A manufacturer recognises an exchange loss on an ordinary pure-financing loan. Applying the same-category rule is not impracticable and no exception applies. Where is that exchange loss generally classified?
options: Financing with the related liability’s income and expenses
Always operating regardless of the underlying item
Directly in OCI under SLFRS 18 itself
explanation: Foreign-exchange differences are generally classified in the same category as income and expenses from the item giving rise to them, subject to the specified exceptions.

title: Tax exchange differences
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. A foreign-exchange difference relates to income tax expense or income within LKAS 12. Which category is specified?
options: Discontinued operations solely because it is foreign currency
explanation: The income-taxes category includes tax expense or income under LKAS 12 and related foreign-exchange differences.

title: Hedge category follows the managed item
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. A designated hedge gain relates to a risk affecting operating expenses. The standard’s same-category conditions are met without prohibited grossing up or other exceptions. Where is the gain classified?
options: Operating, consistently with the affected income and expenses
Financing solely because a derivative is used
Always OCI regardless of the underlying hedge accounting
explanation: Classification of gains and losses on designated hedging instruments follows the affected risk and relevant category requirements, subject to the detailed exceptions. Recognition in profit or loss or OCI is determined separately.

title: PPE disposal versus cash-flow classification
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. A factory machine is used with other resources in manufacturing. The manufacturer recognises a disposal gain. No special rule sends it elsewhere. Does an investing CASH FLOW automatically make this gain investing in profit or loss?
options: No; the gain is generally operating because the machine does not generate independent returns
Yes; profit-or-loss and cash-flow categories must always match
Yes; all non-current-asset gains are financing
No; the gain must always be discontinued operations
explanation: The profit-or-loss categories are not copied from cash-flow classifications. Returns on assets used in combination with other resources are not ordinary independent-asset investing returns.

title: The pre-financing subtotal
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. For an ordinary manufacturer not subject to paragraph 73’s exception, what comprises profit before financing and income taxes?
options: Operating profit plus all investing-category income and expenses
Only revenue less cash-paid operating costs
explanation: The subtotal comprises operating profit and all items in the investing category, subject to the specified exception for certain customer-financing entities.

title: Discontinued operations line
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. A disposal qualifies as a discontinued operation under SLFRS 5. What presentation is required for its total in profit or loss?
options: A single amount for discontinued operations in the designated category
Spread it into every operating line without identifying it
Present it only in the statement of changes in equity
explanation: SLFRS 18 identifies discontinued operations as its own category and requires the single amount specified by SLFRS 5.

title: NCI attribution is not an expense category
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. Where is the allocation of profit or loss to NCI and owners presented?
options: Outside the five profit-or-loss categories as attribution of total profit or loss
As an operating expense deducted before operating profit
explanation: Attribution to NCI and owners is presented outside the five categories. It is not a cost that reduces group profit.

title: Nature and function can coexist
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. An entity considers presenting some operating expense lines by nature and others by function to provide the most useful structured summary. Is a mixture always prohibited?
options: No; both characteristics may be used, but each individual line aggregates on only one basis
Yes; every entity must present all expenses only by function
Yes; every entity must present all expenses only by nature
No; a single line may mix any unrelated aggregation basis without judgment
explanation: The standard permits one or both characteristics while requiring each line item to aggregate on only one of those characteristics.

title: Function presentation needs nature detail
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. An entity presents one or more operating expense lines by function. Which additional single-note disclosure is required?
options: Specified totals for depreciation, amortisation, employee benefits, impairments and inventory write-downs, with required line-item information
Only total cash paid to suppliers
explanation: Paragraph 83 specifies the five nature-based totals and the information linking them to line items when operating function lines are presented.

title: No extraordinary category
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. Management describes a large loss as extraordinary and proposes a sixth mandatory category for it. What is appropriate?
options: Apply the five categories and the relevant presentation and material-disaggregation requirements
Create a mandatory extraordinary category whenever management uses that word
Always move the loss to OCI
Exclude the loss from all financial statements
explanation: The standard specifies five profit-or-loss categories. Labels such as unusual or extraordinary do not establish an additional mandatory category or override classification.

title: Aggregation must not obscure
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. Several material expenses have dissimilar characteristics but are combined into an unexplained other line. What principle applies?
options: Disaggregate as needed so material information is not obscured
Combine them whenever the total is mathematically correct
Omit descriptions if management prefers secrecy
Use one other line for every material event
explanation: Aggregation and disaggregation follow shared or dissimilar characteristics and must not obscure material information.

title: Net ECL is not prohibited offsetting
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. A receivable is measured net of its expected-credit-loss allowance. Is this net measurement automatically the offsetting prohibited by the standard?
options: No; measuring assets net of valuation allowances is not offsetting
Yes; all valuation allowances are prohibited netting
Yes; gross assets and allowance must always be separate primary line items
No; therefore all unrelated assets and liabilities may be netted
explanation: The standard distinguishes net asset measurement using valuation allowances from offsetting unrelated recognised items.

title: Labels must describe the measure
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. A subtotal includes financing amounts but is labelled profit before financing. What is the relevant concern?
options: The label must faithfully represent the included amounts and not imply financing is excluded
Any label is acceptable if used in a press release
Financing amounts must be relabelled as revenue
Misleading labels are permitted in notes
explanation: Items and subtotals must be clearly and faithfully described. The standard specifically restricts misleading pre-financing labels in the applicable exception.

title: A cash-flow metric is not an MPM subtotal
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. A public communication uses free cash flow. The metric is a cash-flow measure rather than a subtotal of income and expenses. Does that fact alone make it a management-defined performance measure under this definition?
options: No; the definition requires a subtotal of income and expenses
Yes; every publicly communicated metric is an MPM
Yes; every number outside financial statements is an MPM
No; cash flows may never be discussed publicly
explanation: MPMs are qualifying subtotals of income and expenses. Cash-flow measures and other metrics outside that definition do not become MPMs simply by being public.

title: Internal-only subtotal
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. A subtotal is used only in internal budgets and is never used in public communications outside the financial statements. Does it meet the stated public-communication criterion for an MPM?
options: No; that criterion is not met on these facts
Yes; any internal spreadsheet subtotal is an MPM
Yes; every budget amount is an MPM
Only if its amount exceeds a fixed percentage of profit
explanation: The definition includes use in public communications outside the financial statements, along with the other specified conditions.

title: Specified subtotal is excluded from MPMs
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. An entity publicly reports operating profit before depreciation, amortisation and impairments within LKAS 36. Does the specified subtotal automatically become an MPM?
options: No; that exact subtotal is listed among those excluded from the MPM definition
Yes; it must always be an MPM regardless of the exclusion
Yes; every EBITDA-like label has identical mandatory treatment
No; therefore additional adjustments to it can never produce an MPM
explanation: The listed subtotal is excluded. A differently adjusted subtotal still requires assessment against the MPM definition.

title: All MPMs in one note
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. An entity has three qualifying MPMs. How should the required MPM information be organised?
options: In a single note covering all qualifying MPMs
In three unrelated notes with no required explanation
explanation: All measures meeting the MPM definition are disclosed in a single note, including the prescribed management-view and comparability statement.

title: Tax and NCI per reconciling item
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. An MPM reconciliation has multiple reconciling items. What additional effects must be disclosed for each item?
options: Its income tax effect and effect on NCI
No item-level effects if a net total is given
explanation: The reconciliation requires income tax and NCI effects for each reconciling item, together with the specified explanation of the tax-effect method.

title: Changing an MPM calculation
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. An entity changes how it calculates an MPM. What is generally required?
options: Explain the change and reasons, and restate comparative information unless impracticable
Change it silently because it is a management measure
Never provide comparative information for management measures
explanation: The standard specifies explanation, reasons and comparative restatement for changes, additions or cessation, with an impracticability exception and disclosure.

title: MPM selection is not a policy choice
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. An entity changes its selection of MPM. Is selection itself an accounting policy choice?
options: No; the standard says it is not, although the specified LKAS 8 impracticability guidance is used
Yes; every MPM selection is a measurement policy under SLFRS 9
Yes; it changes recognition of all underlying transactions
No; therefore no change disclosures are ever needed
explanation: Selection of an MPM is not an accounting policy choice. Nonetheless the specified guidance applies in judging impracticability for comparative restatement.

title: Notes do not repair a poor primary summary
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. Management omits information necessary for the primary statements’ useful structured summary, arguing that a long note automatically cures the omission. Which principle applies?
options: Primary statements and notes have distinct complementary roles that must both be fulfilled
A note always replaces any required primary presentation
Only notes matter for every financial statement user
Primary statements may omit all required subtotals
explanation: The roles of primary statements and notes are distinct. Required primary presentation and useful structured summaries cannot be bypassed merely by adding a note.

title: Explain a specified main business activity
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. An entity concludes it invests in assets as a main business activity. What explicit disclosure follows?
options: Never disclose it because it is management judgment
Disclose only the company’s legal name
Disclose it only if the activity makes a loss
explanation: The standard requires disclosure when the entity invests in assets or provides financing to customers as a main business activity, and specified information when the assessment outcome changes.

title: Earnings measures do not change recognition
prompt: Apply the SLFRS 18. A management-defined subtotal excludes a restructuring expense. Does including that adjustment in an MPM remove the underlying expense from the SLFRS financial statements?
options: No; MPM disclosure does not override recognition and classification under the standards
Yes; every MPM adjustment cancels the underlying journal entry
Yes; management measures override provisions accounting
Only if the adjustment raises operating profit
explanation: MPMs explain management’s view through transparent disclosures and reconciliations; they do not replace the accounting requirements for the underlying transactions.

title: Return recovery asset net of costs • case 1
prompt: A retailer has transferred 1,025 products. It expects 41 to be returned. Each returned product originally cost LKR 600; expected recovery handling is 20 per item and expected value deterioration is 30 per item. Estimates meet the relevant requirements. Find the separate asset for the right to recover returned products, excluding the refund liability.
explanation: Recovery asset = original carrying amount of expected returns less recovery costs and potential value decrease: 41 × (600 − 20 − 30) = 22,550.00. It is assessed separately from the customer refund liability.
family: Return recovery asset net of costs

title: Retrospective volume rebate true-up • case 1
prompt: A customer’s annual purchases reach 10,100 units at list price LKR 200. Crossing the threshold entitles it to a 5% retrospective rebate on ALL units. Cumulative revenue before this new supported estimate equals full list price; no rebate was previously accrued. The constraint permits the estimate. Find the reduction in cumulative revenue required now.
explanation: The revised transaction price reflects the retrospective rebate on all units. Revenue reduction = 10,100 × 200 × 5% = 101,000.00. Recognise the corresponding refund obligation as appropriate.

title: Discount specifically allocated to one obligation • case 1
prompt: A bundle has distinct goods A and B with stand-alone prices LKR 205,000 and 310,000. Total transaction price is 464,000. ALL paragraph 82 criteria demonstrate that the whole 51,000 discount relates only to A. A transfers now; B is not yet delivered. Find revenue recognised for A.
explanation: The specified discount-allocation exception applies. Allocate all 51,000 discount to A: 205,000 − 51,000 = 154,000.00. Do not default to relative allocation when the exception’s criteria are met.
family: Discount specifically allocated to one obligation

title: Three obligations and partial service • case 1
prompt: A contract price of LKR 1,230,000 covers goods A, goods B and twelve months of distinct support. Stand-alone prices are 600,000, 300,000 and 300,000 respectively. A is delivered, B is not, and six months of evenly provided support are complete. No allocation exception applies. Find cumulative revenue.
explanation: Recognise allocation to A plus half of support: 1,230,000 × (600,000 + 150,000) / 1,200,000 = 768,750.00. B’s allocation remains unrecognised as revenue.

title: Progress excluding abnormal waste • case 1
prompt: An over-time contract has transaction price LKR 10,100,000. Costs incurred are 4,040,000, including abnormal waste of 202,000 that does not depict progress. Expected TOTAL productive costs excluding that waste are 8,080,000. Cost-to-cost is appropriate after excluding the waste; no other adjustment applies. Find cumulative revenue, not profit.
explanation: Exclude abnormal waste from the progress numerator. Productive progress = (4,040,000 − 202,000) / 8,080,000. Revenue = transaction price × that progress = 4,797,500.00. The wasted cost is not a revenue-producing input.

title: Uninstalled materials without margin • case 1
prompt: A single over-time construction obligation has price LKR 10,200,000. All B19(b) conditions justify recognising revenue equal to cost for significant uninstalled materials of 2,040,000 already controlled by the customer. Other productive costs incurred are 1,530,000; expected total OTHER costs are 6,120,000. No revenue was previously recognised. Find cumulative revenue.
explanation: Recognise material revenue without margin: 2,040,000. Recognise the remaining price using other-cost progress: (10,200,000 − 2,040,000) × 1,530,000/6,120,000. Total revenue = 4,080,000.00.

title: Agent commission after collection • case 1
prompt: An intermediary is an AGENT and collects customer cash of LKR 1,050,000 for a completed supplier service. It must remit 88% to the supplier and is entitled to the remaining 12% commission. It controls neither the underlying service nor any distinct extra service, and there is no tax. Find its revenue.
explanation: An agent recognises its fee or commission, not the supplier’s gross billings: 1,050,000 × 12% = 126,000.00. The amount due to the supplier is separately accounted for.

title: Distinct remaining goods blended prospectively • case 1
prompt: At modification, 100 distinct goods remain under an existing contract at LKR 1,010 each. Another 50 distinct goods are added at 808 each. The modification is NOT a separate contract, but remaining goods are distinct from those already transferred, so paragraph 21(a) applies prospectively. Thirty of the remaining goods are then transferred. Find revenue for those thirty.
explanation: Prospective remaining consideration = 100 × 1,010 + 50 × 808. Divide by 150 remaining goods, then multiply by 30 = 28,280.00. Do not retrospectively revise revenue on goods already transferred.

title: FVTPL acquisition expense • case 1
prompt: A financial asset is acquired at fair value LKR 820,000 and is classified at FVTPL. Directly attributable broker costs are 20,500, paid separately. No fair-value change occurs immediately after purchase. Find the immediate profit-or-loss expense from acquiring this asset.
explanation: Transaction costs on an FVTPL asset are expensed. Initial asset carrying amount is fair value 820,000; immediate acquisition expense is 20,500.00.

title: Collateral cash-shortfall discounting • case 1
prompt: A credit loss scenario has a contractual receipt of LKR 1,025,000 due in one year. The ONLY expected recovery at that same date is collateral sale proceeds of 715,000, less sale costs of 51,000. Scenario probability is 100% and original EIR is 10%. Collateral is an integral contractual credit enhancement and not separately recognised. Find discounted ECL.
explanation: One-year shortfall = contractual receipt − net collateral recovery = 1,025,000 − (715,000 − 51,000). Discount that shortfall at 10%: 328,181.82. Do not ignore recovery costs or discount only one side of same-date cash flows.

title: Three-band provision matrix • case 1
prompt: Under the simplified lifetime-ECL approach, supported adjusted loss rates are 1% on current receivables of LKR 1,020,000, 5% on past-due balances of 305,000, and 30% on severely overdue balances of 102,000. Rates already include all required forward-looking and discounting effects. Find total loss allowance.
explanation: Apply each appropriate band rate and add: 1,020,000×1% + 305,000×5% + 102,000×30% = 56,050.00. Do not apply one blended band mechanically to all balances.

title: Equity FVOCI profit-or-loss dividend • case 1
